content: Psoriasis is a chronic dermatological condition that affects approximately 2% of the general population. The most prevalent form, plaque psoriasis, is characterized by raised, erythematous patches of inflamed skin covered with silvery-white scales. These lesions often present in a symmetrical distribution. Guttate psoriasis, a distinct subtype, manifests as numerous small, erythematosquamous lesions. Streptococcal infections are hypothesized to play a role in triggering the onset of guttate psoriasis and exacerbating chronic plaque psoriasis. The last Cochrane Review on this topic, published in 2000, necessitated an update due to the continued use of antistreptococcal treatments, particularly for acute guttate psoriasis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of antistreptococcal interventions, such as tonsillectomy or systemic antibiotic therapy, in managing guttate and chronic plaque psoriasis. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing these interventions to placebo, no treatment, or alternative treatments. The primary outcomes assessed were the time to resolution of psoriasis and the proportion of participants achieving clear or almost clear skin, as defined by the Physician Global Assessment (PGA) or Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI). Secondary outcomes included the proportion of participants achieving partial improvement (PASI 75 or PGA 1-2), the risk of relapse at long-term follow-up, and the incidence of adverse events. The review identified five trials involving 162 participants, with ages ranging from 12 to 77 years. Only two participants were under 15 years of age. Baseline PASI scores ranged from mild (5.7) to severe (23). Twenty-three participants had positive throat cultures for streptococcus. Due to heterogeneity in participant characteristics and interventions, a meta-analysis was not performed. None of the trials measured the primary outcome of time to resolution or the secondary outcome of relapse risk at long-term follow-up. The overall quality of evidence was rated as very low due to high risks of bias, including lack of blinding and outcome reporting bias, as well as imprecision stemming from small sample sizes and limited events. Consequently, the results are highly uncertain. For guttate psoriasis, one three-arm trial (N=43) compared penicillin (50,000 IU/kg/day in three doses), erythromycin (250 mg four times daily), and no treatment over 14 days, with a six-week follow-up. This study did not measure adverse events or the proportion of participants achieving clear or almost clear skin. Another trial (N=20) compared intramuscular penicillin (1.6 million units daily) to no treatment over six weeks, with an eight-week follow-up. No adverse events were reported, and there was no statistically significant difference in the proportion of participants achieving clear or almost clear skin (RR 2.00, 95% CI 0.68 to 5.85). A third trial (N=20) compared rifampicin (300 mg twice daily) to placebo over 14 days, with a six-week follow-up, but none of the review outcomes were measured. None of these trials assessed the proportion of participants achieving PASI 75 or PGA 1-2. For chronic plaque psoriasis, one trial (N=50) compared long-term azithromycin (500 mg daily) to vitamin C over 48 weeks. Adverse events, including nausea and mild abdominal discomfort, were reported in 10 of 30 participants in the azithromycin group, but not in the vitamin C group. The proportion of participants achieving clear or almost clear skin was not measured. However, 18 of 30 participants in the azithromycin group achieved PASI 75, compared to none in the vitamin C group (RR 25.06, 95% CI 1.60 to 393.59). Another trial (N=29) compared tonsillectomy to no treatment, with a 24-month follow-up. One participant in the tonsillectomy group experienced minor bleeding. At eight weeks, 1 of 15 participants in the tonsillectomy group achieved PASI 90, compared to none in the no-treatment group. Additionally, 3 of 15 participants in the tonsillectomy group achieved PASI 75, compared to none in the no-treatment group (RR 6.56, 95% CI 0.37 to 116.7). In conclusion, the review included five trials evaluating systemic antibiotics (penicillin, azithromycin) and tonsillectomy for guttate and chronic plaque psoriasis. Two comparisons (erythromycin vs. no treatment and rifampicin vs. placebo) did not measure any of the outcomes of interest. The evidence for the measured outcomes was of very low quality, leaving the efficacy and safety of antistreptococcal interventions uncertain. The included studies were limited by small sample sizes, high or unclear risks of bias, and inadequate measurement of key outcomes. Additionally, the role of streptococcal infection in psoriasis and the efficacy of amoxicillin, a commonly used antibiotic, were not addressed. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness and tolerability of penicillin V or amoxicillin in children and young adults with guttate psoriasis.
